body: Need for Speed III: Hot Pursuit is a 1998 racing video game developed for PlayStation by EA Canada and Microsoft Windows by EA Seattle, and published by Electronic Arts. It is the third major installment in the Need for Speed franchise, incorporating police pursuits as a major part of gameplay. Hot Pursuit remains focused on racing using exotic sports cars, but features races that primarily take place in locations within North America, including varied settings and climates. Police AI is improved over the first game, utilizing several tactics to stop both the player and opponent. The PlayStation version was released on March 25, 1998, while the Windows version was released on September 23, the same year. The game received critical success, with praise for its graphics and customization options. It received a direct sequel in 2002 and a reboot in 2010.

old_entry.title: Brave Fencer Musashi
old_entry.subtitle: Brave Fencer Musashi Brings Action Rhythm into Square's RPG
old_entry.summary: On July 16, 1998 Square released Brave Fencer Musashi for PlayStation in Japan.
body: On July 16, 1998 Square released Brave Fencer Musashi for PlayStation in Japan. At a time when the company was identified mainly with large turn-based RPGs, Musashi chose real-time combat, jumping, three-dimensional exploration and a world governed by a day-night cycle. The Fusion ability also lets the hero absorb techniques from enemies, turning opponents into sources of tools. The game shows a Square willing to use its narrative and production expertise from JRPGs to build an adventure that is more physical, comic and immediate.

Musashi is a platform game in which the title character, Musashi, fights a variety of enemies using his swords Fusion and Lumina and searches for five scrolls which will increase Lumina's strength and grant him new abilities. There are also several minigames and puzzles scattered throughout which must be completed to advance the plot. The two swords he uses have varied abilities and uses. Fusion, which resembles a katana, is used to chain rapid combo hits together and can also be used to absorb Bincho energy, which is a type of magical point system that controls how many spells a player can cast and how quickly, or absorb an enemies' skill. Lumina is a large, double-edged weapon which cannot be effectively used in combos by itself; instead, it can be imbued with elemental properties from Scrolls. Lumina is primarily offensive but in combination with the five elemental scrolls, it gains new skills. The two swords can be used in conjunction with certain techniques which are granted by various rescued townsfolk.

Executive producer Hironobu Sakaguchi stated that the idea for the game first came up in February 1997. The original idea for Brave Fencer Musashi was having Miyamoto Musashi fighting in an alternate world from where he belonged. While the game was conceptualized as action-oriented, Musashi was originally meant to be a wanderer, but was later changed to an itinerant Samaritan in order to have him interacting and helping other characters. During development, the team used an action base which was crucial to the game's fighting mechanics. Director Yoichi Yoshimoto focused on the game's fully polygonal aspects that were a departure from Square's previous works. The development team prioritized the movement of polygons in real time and how light affected their appearance.

The player can either go to an inn to recover Musashi's health or make Musashi sleep outdoors without a full recovery and with danger he may be attacked by enemies. To pass time, the player may also opt to collect the various action figures – which resemble more detailed models of nearly all the characters and monsters – available at the town toy store, which stocks new items at the start of every chapter. Along the way, Musashi obtains parts from the Legendary Armor which allow him to perform actions such as climbing or performing double jumps.

old_entry.title: Metal Gear Solid
old_entry.subtitle: Stealth meets cinema without losing sight of play
old_entry.summary: Konami released Metal Gear Solid in Japan for PlayStation on September 3, 1998.
body: Konami released Metal Gear Solid in Japan for PlayStation on September 3, 1998. The game brings Kojima's MSX stealth idea into 3D, but does far more than replace sprites with polygons. Camera, vision cones, radar, sound and codec conversations turn information into a resource to be read. Shadow Moses is compact enough to memorize and theatrical enough to change meaning as the story advances. Boss encounters and interface tricks repeatedly break the boundary between what happens to the character and what the player is physically doing with the console and controller. Metal Gear Solid therefore became one of the works that defined PlayStation: cinematic, certainly, but above all sharply aware that it was a video game.

Metal Gear Solid brings three-dimensional stealth to PlayStation without giving up clarity. The Soliton radar shows guard positions and fields of vision, allowing players to read a room even when the camera cannot frame every threat. It is not a shortcut that removes tension: it forces attention to move between physical space and an abstract representation. When an alert begins, the radar changes state and the same room suddenly becomes more dangerous. Shadow Moses is therefore understood through two simultaneous images, the cinematic view of the world and the tactical view of the interface. Stealth emerges from the relationship between them.

The codec lets Snake speak with Colonel Campbell, Naomi, Mei Ling and others without physically leaving the mission area. The screen reduces the world to two portraits, a frequency and a voice, radically changing the rhythm after a stretch of infiltration. These conversations deliver instructions, biographies, jokes, technical explanations and moral doubts. The codec is therefore tutorial, radio drama and narrative archive at once. Kojima can include extensive writing without building a new three-dimensional scene every time. The result gives the mission unusual density: the player is alone in the field but is almost never truly isolated.

Psycho Mantis remains memorable because the encounter does not stay inside the rules of the room. The character comments on certain information stored on the memory card and appears to anticipate player inputs, eventually pointing toward a solution involving the controller port. The effect uses the PlayStation itself as dramatic material: hardware and personal data become part of the staging. The trick works because it arrives after hours in which the player has learned to trust the game's conventions. Those conventions are suddenly displaced. Metal Gear Solid shows that a console is not only the technical support for a work but can become one of its narrative objects.

editorial_features.title: Looking through a miniature room
editorial_features.summary: Kojima and Shinkawa negotiated what players could see.
body: Graph paper did not tell Kojima everything he needed to know about a room. During Metal Gear Solid's development, a column could hide a doorway that seemed perfectly visible in a plan. The team built structures from toy blocks and inspected them with a miniature camera. Their models tested what Snake could actually see from inside the space. The exercise made the switch to three dimensions tangible: a plausible floor plan was not yet a readable environment for a person moving through it.

In that prerelease interview, Kojima also described suspense carried by sound. Hearing leaves crushed without knowing the source had frightened him in other games; he wanted comparable uncertainty in Metal Gear Solid. This was an intention, not a measurement of every player's reaction. It identifies a different task from simply displaying a threat. The player must judge incomplete evidence, deciding whether movement is safe before the source becomes visible. Sight and hearing were being considered together as ways to withhold useful information.

Yoji Shinkawa worked out Metal Gear REX as a physical object, building a model from scratch. Kojima remembered requesting a weapon that suggested a dinosaur when operated, without looking like a visiting spacecraft. As the model took shape, computer artists developed the digital version alongside it. The physical reference therefore belonged inside a continuing production exchange. It was neither a decorative sculpture made after the game nor proof that the director's initial description already contained every contour of the machine's eventual form.

editorial_features.title: Looking through a miniature room
editorial_features.summary: Kojima and Shinkawa negotiated what players could see.
body: Graph paper did not tell Kojima everything he needed to know about a room. During Metal Gear Solid's development, a column could hide a doorway that seemed perfectly visible in a plan. The exercise made the switch to three dimensions tangible: a plausible floor plan was not yet a readable environment for a person moving through it.

Hearing leaves crushed without knowing the source had frightened him in other games; he wanted comparable uncertainty in Metal Gear Solid. The player must judge incomplete evidence, deciding whether movement is safe before the source becomes visible. old_entry.title: SoulCalibur
old_entry.subtitle: SoulCalibur Makes Eight-Way Movement a New Grammar for the Duel
old_entry.summary: On July 30, 1998 Namco released SoulCalibur in arcades.
body: On July 30, 1998 Namco released SoulCalibur in arcades. Weapons distinguish reach, rhythm and space, but the clearest breakthrough is three-dimensional movement: the 8-Way Run makes circling an opponent feel natural and turns the arena into territory to control. The arcade game came before the celebrated Dreamcast conversion that would expand its reputation. Even here, SoulCalibur shows how a fighting game can pursue spectacle without sacrificing readability, precision or the identity of individual styles.

One of the biggest innovations introduced by Soulcalibur to the gameplay system of its predecessor, Soul Edge, is the eight-way run. Previous 3D fighters had only limited movement along the third axis, with sidesteps and rolls providing useful but unsustained lateral movement. In Soulcalibur, simply holding down a joystick direction causes the character to move in that direction, giving the player a sense of freedom and deepening the strategy of the game.

Yotoriyama has described the game's concept as expressing "fun and diversity in weapon combat", citing the contrast in how one weapon would affect gameplay compared to another and how they would react to each other upon clashing. Each character's fighting style was designed to revolve around their weapon, though he noted that because of the differences they experienced difficulty in balancing the gameplay. He described the availability of movement in comparison to Tekken 3 as a large contrast between the two series and more tactical and emphasized how it interacted with the game's "ring out" feature. Each character in Soulcalibur was designed around the idea that they could be viewed as a real person could, and to this end, motion creator Masataka Ishiguro emphasized the arm and leg movements for each character in relation to their weapon, wanting players to "feel the individual motions and the realism within the game"

The Dreamcast version of Soulcalibur is one of the first examples of a home conversion of a game being graphically superior to its original arcade counterpart. Among the differences were the improved graphics (including the addition of 3D backgrounds), tweaked gameplay, new game modes, new costumes, and the inclusion of an extra character, Cervantes de Leon. The Dreamcast version features new modes such as Team Battle, Survival, and Training Mode. In Mission Battle, the player completes various missions to attain points, which can be used to buy various art, which then unlocks extra features, costumes and stages. Another feature added is the artwork section, containing official artwork, fanart, and high-res pictures. Also unlockable are a "liquid metal" version of the characters' costume and a "Battle Theater" mode, plus a way to modify the opening introduction theme by changing the characters appearing in it, and an "Exhibition Mode" displaying characters performing their katas (in Mission Mode it is possible to add more characters to the "Exhibition Mode", such as Taki and Seung Mina).

source_paragraphs: The Dreamcast version of Soulcalibur is one of the first examples of a home conversion of a game being graphically superior to its original arcade counterpart. Among the differences were the improved graphics (including the addition of 3D backgrounds), tweaked gameplay, new game modes, new costumes, and the inclusion of an extra character, Cervantes de Leon. The Dreamcast version features new modes such as Team Battle, Survival, and Training Mode. In Mission Battle, the player completes various missions to attain points, which can be used to buy various art, which then unlocks extra features, costumes and stages. Another feature added is the artwork section, containing official artwork, fanart, and high-res pictures. Also unlockable are a "liquid metal" version of the characters' costume and a "Battle Theater" mode, plus a way to modify the opening introduction theme by changing the characters appearing in it, and an "Exhibition Mode" displaying characters performing their katas (in Mission Mode it is possible to add more characters to the "Exhibition Mode", such as Taki and Seung Mina).

old_entry.title: Tom Clancy's Rainbow Six
old_entry.summary: Tom Clancy's Rainbow Six is a 1998 tactical shooter video game developed and published by Red Storm Entertainment for Microsoft Windows, with later ports for the Nintendo 64, PlayStation, Mac OS, Game Boy Color, and Dreamcast.
body: Tom Clancy's Rainbow Six is a 1998 tactical shooter video game developed and published by Red Storm Entertainment for Microsoft Windows, with later ports for the Nintendo 64, PlayStation, Mac OS, Game Boy Color, and Dreamcast. It is the first installment in the Rainbow Six series. Based on the Tom Clancy novel of the same name, the game follows Rainbow, a top secret international counterterrorist organization, and the conspiracy they unravel as they handle a seemingly random spike in terrorism.

In singleplayer, the player advances through a series of missions in a campaign. Before each mission, the player is briefed on the situation, selects and organizes their operatives and equipment, and plans their movement through the level; during missions, the player controls an operative leading computer-controlled teammates as they follow the player's plan. In multiplayer, players cooperate in player-versus-environment missions or battle to complete objectives in player-versus-player matches. The game features realistic gameplay factors, weapon lethality, and consequences for failure, forcing players to plan their approach carefully and promoting replayability for more streamlined completion.

Rainbow Six began as a concept by Red Storm following their formation in 1996. The game was developed in parallel with the Rainbow Six novel, with a design philosophy of realism and strategy guiding all aspects of development; however, numerous setbacks stymied the game's development and forced the developers to crunch. Though his name is in the game's title, Tom Clancy's involvement in Rainbow Six's development was very minimal. Red Storm developed the PC version, while all other ports were developed by their respective companies.

Rainbow Six was released on August 21, 1998 to widespread critical acclaim, though the console ports received relatively lower ratings than the PC version. For most releases, praise was directed toward gameplay, multiplayer, immersion, and the game's combination of strategy and action, while criticism mainly centered on AI issues, glitches, and the graphics and controls of some ports. The game sold over 200,000 copies in its first year of release and continued to sell hundreds of thousands more copies well into the early 2000s. Rainbow Six was nominated for numerous accolades and has been deemed one of the best video games of 1998. It is considered a milestone in the history of first-person shooters and made a lasting impact on the then-fledgling tactical shooter genre.

An expansion pack, Tom Clancy's Rainbow Six Mission Pack: Eagle Watch, was released on January 26, 1999. A sequel, Tom Clancy's Rainbow Six: Rogue Spear, was released in 1999. A loose mobile game remake, Tom Clancy's Rainbow Six: Shadow Vanguard, was released in 2011.

old_entry.title: Grim Fandango
old_entry.subtitle: Even the Afterlife Has a Service Counter
old_entry.summary: On October 30, 1998, Grim Fandango reached US stores for Windows, after LucasArts had begun shipping it in the preceding days.
body: On October 30, 1998, Grim Fandango reached US stores for Windows, after LucasArts had begun shipping it in the preceding days. Tim Schafer and the team turn the graphic adventure into a meeting of Mexican folklore, Día de Muertos imagery, modernist architecture, and the language of noir. Manny Calavera is an employee of the afterlife, but the game's strength lies less in the premise than in the way environments, dialogue, puzzles, and music make an impossible world feel coherent. Technically, LucasArts abandons the traditional 2D animation of its adventure games for three-dimensional characters placed in prerendered backgrounds and adopts direct keyboard control. It is a choice that changes the relationship with space and anticipates the genre's need to rethink interface and direction in the 3D era.

Grim Fandango's art direction brings together sources that could have remained simple quotations. The skeletal figures evoke Día de Muertos, while buildings, offices, casinos, and vehicles absorb modernist geometry, Mesoamerican motifs, and film-noir shadows. The result does not simply decorate a detective story with skulls. The Land of the Dead has its own bureaucracy, economy, means of transportation, and workplaces, so every visual reference is translated into function. GameSpot's contemporary review noted how Latin American sources were used to build architecture and machines believable within that universe. This coherence allows the game to change city and atmosphere without losing identity. Manny remains an immediately readable silhouette, while the setting can move from office to port to casino while preserving the same balance of elegance, death, and everyday life.

With Grim Fandango, LucasArts abandons traditional two-dimensional animation in its adventure games for the first time and adopts 3D characters within prerendered backgrounds. The interface changes too: the mouse and visible verbs give way to direct keyboard control, while Manny turns his head toward significant objects to indicate that they can be examined. It is a solution that moves part of the interface into the character's animation. The player has to observe Manny's body and the framing, not only a cursor. This transition also brings orientation problems, because fixed cameras and three-dimensional movement can make exits and directions ambiguous. Precisely for this reason, the game is an important document of 1998: it shows a historic genre trying to redefine its tools for a 3D environment before point-and-click returned in different forms.

In graphic adventures, the risk is that a puzzle feels like a lock placed in front of the story. Grim Fandango instead tries to make narrative objectives and logical problems coincide: obtaining information, convincing a character, or reaching a place requires chains of actions involving objects and relationships already present in the environment. GameSpot's 1998 review specifically emphasized the integration of puzzles into the plot and the variety of solutions, often made up of several steps. This approach allows comedy to grow from character behavior rather than separate gags. When a solution works, the player has not simply found the correct combination: they have understood something about the social rules of that bureaucratic afterlife. Even the difficulty, sometimes severe, comes from this density of relationships. The puzzle thus becomes a characterization tool rather than an interruption between two dialogue scenes.

Grim Fandango knows noir well enough not to reduce it to a series of jokes about a detective in a trench coat. GameSpot already observed in 1998 that the writing evoked works such as Casablanca, Chinatown, and Glengarry Glen Ross, but built its humor mainly through situations and characters. Manny speaks like a weary professional inside an absurd system, and it is precisely the seriousness with which he accepts the bureaucracy of the afterlife that makes the jokes believable. Supporting characters also have distinct rhythms, ambitions, and registers, supported by the voice acting. The writing does not have to continually explain the strangeness of the world because environments and rules have already made it normal. This balance is central to the game's tone: noir provides a structure of desires, betrayals, and corruption, while comedy prevents the homage from becoming rigid imitation. The result remains recognizable without depending on a single parody.

Grim Fandango's sound contributes to distinguishing places and cultures as much as its architecture does. Peter McConnell composes a score that, according to GameSpot's contemporary review, moves through jazz and mariachi without treating them as simple labels. The voice cast, led by Tony Plana as Manny, gives dialogue timing and inflections that support the tone between noir, comedy, and melancholy. The original credits also list a sound department and the iMUSE system, LucasArts' technological legacy for interactive music management. Music, voices, and effects are therefore not a finishing layer applied at the end. They help make Rubacava feel different from El Marrow and make characters recognizable even before the plot fully defines them. Audio builds emotional continuity in a game that changes city, year, and atmosphere, tying Manny's long journey to a coherent sonic memory.

Grim Fandango's production history is unusually readable because, years later, Double Fine recovered diaries, original materials, and testimony from the team while working on Remastered. Among these documents are the notes Tim Schafer wrote in 1998 for the official strategy guide. Their value is not in turning the original game into a museum curiosity, but in showing how much a production depends on everyday decisions, tools, and compromises that the final software tends to hide. Reconstructing the work also required searching for nearly lost assets and consulting people who had taken part in the project. This story makes Grim Fandango a useful case for discussing preservation: preserving the executable alone is not enough to explain why an image, control, or sound took that form. Development materials restore the process alongside the result.

old_entry.title: Pokémon Yellow
old_entry.subtitle: A Companion Walks Outside the Ball
old_entry.summary: On September 12, 1998, Nintendo released Pocket Monsters Pikachu in Japan, known outside the country as Pokémon Yellow.
body: On September 12, 1998, Nintendo released Pocket Monsters Pikachu in Japan, known outside the country as Pokémon Yellow. It is a new version of Pokémon Red and Green, built on the same Kanto region but enriched with events and references that bring the game closer to the hugely popular animated series. The most immediate difference is physical: Pikachu does not remain confined to the party or the menu, but follows the protagonist on screen. Talking to it reveals its mood, while its cry uses the voice made familiar by the anime. Yellow also arrives in the year of the first Pokémon film and remains compatible with trading in Red, Green and Blue. It is an update that shows how the same adventure can change meaning by altering primarily the relationship with the companion.

In Red and Green, the first Pokémon exists mainly in the menu, in battles and in the player's imagination. Yellow brings Pikachu out of that separation and has it walk behind the protagonist. It is a small technical change but an enormous perceptual one. Turning around and talking to Pikachu reveals different expressions tied to its mood, so the bond is communicated not only through statistics or dialogue. The creature occupies the same route, passes through towns and roads and becomes a recurring presence in the routine of the journey. The game does not simulate complex behavior, but it provides enough signals for the player to read closeness, annoyance or excitement. It is a lesson in interactive character design: changing where a character appears can change how much it seems to live beside us.

Pokémon Yellow also changes how Pikachu sounds. The official Virtual Console release notes that its cry uses the voice from the animated series instead of being limited to the synthetic tone normally used to identify creatures in the first generation. On Game Boy, this choice has particular value: a recognizable voice enters a very spare sound environment and creates an immediate link with the Pikachu from television. There is no need to reproduce a scene from the anime to create continuity between the two media. A short sound, repeated throughout the adventure, is enough to shift the companion's identity. Voice thus becomes a technology of recognition. The character audiences hear every week can now respond directly to the player's action within the limits of a handheld cartridge.

By 1998, Pokémon is no longer only a series of cartridges. The anime began in Japan in 1997, and the first film, Mewtwo Strikes Back, reached theaters in July 1998. Nintendo presented Pocket Monsters Pikachu as a release connected to that cinematic moment as well. Yellow takes advantage of this expansion without becoming a simple adaptation of the episodes: Kanto remains a region to explore according to role-playing rules, but some encounters and characterizations feel more familiar to viewers of the animated series. It is an important step in the history of the franchise. The video game, origin of the entire phenomenon, begins in turn to absorb elements from the success of other media. The relationship no longer runs in a single direction: television, cinema, merchandise and cartridge feed one another.

Pokémon Yellow preserves almost the entire narrative structure of Red and Green, but introduces new events and changes the way the player relates to Kanto. This continuity is essential: anyone who already knows the region can anticipate towns, routes and Gyms, and therefore notices every difference more precisely. A new version does not have to replace the previous world completely in order to matter. It can work through comparison, turning the player's memory into design material. Pikachu following behind makes every return immediately different, while encounters and references tied to the anime's popularity shift the emphasis of certain scenes. Yellow therefore shows a model Pokémon would use often: keep a recognizable structure and change selected points so that a familiar route is reinterpreted rather than simply repeated.

A variant could have isolated buyers from the audience of the earlier cartridges. Pokémon Yellow instead keeps trading with Red, Green and Blue through the Game Link Cable. Compatibility preserves the social principle on which Pokémon was built: no single cartridge easily contains the entire ecosystem, and collecting gains value when it passes between people. The new game therefore enters an existing community instead of forcing it to start over. This is especially important in 1998, when the series is expanding rapidly through anime, cards and merchandise, yet the act of trading still depends on two Game Boys physically connected to one another. Yellow adds individual value to Pikachu as a companion without abandoning the collective structure that made the first generation distinctive.

The idea of a Pokémon walking beside the protagonist does not remain confined to 1998. When Nintendo discusses the production of HeartGold and SoulSilver, it recalls Yellow as a version of Red and Green to which additional value had been added, including Pikachu following the player. In later years the series would return repeatedly to that relationship between creature and space, extending it to other Pokémon and new hardware. The reason for its persistence is already legible in the original: a visible companion reduces the distance between what the player feels they own and what they see inhabiting the world. A statistic can explain how strong a creature is; a presence beside the avatar instead suggests how much time has been shared. Yellow thus turns a limited technical variation into a lasting emotional memory.

body: StarCraft set three distinct forces against one another, requiring players to manage production, information and movement at once. Its multiplayer depth made learning an ongoing activity rather than something completed by finishing a campaign.

In South Korea, PC rooms, organised competition and broadcasts helped make the game a public spectacle. That development cannot be explained by software alone: places to play, network infrastructure, commentators and audiences built the culture around it.

editorial_features.title: A room for playing and watching
editorial_features.summary: Watching and playing share a room.
body: Kook Kibong, known as TheBOy, recalls first finding his friends playing StarCraft in an internet café in Australia in 1998. He returned to watch before beginning himself. In Blizzard's later interview, this encounter sits beside memories of competing at Daytona USA machines and studying how to shave fractions from a lap time. The route into a strategy game did not begin with an isolated purchase. Other people, an available machine and the opportunity to watch made a new kind of play visible to him.

Kibong describes building a reputation on Battle.net, acquiring a manager and sponsor, and preparing strategies through repeated games and written notes. His memory of Korea's 1999 competitive scene includes television appearances and a first live tournament. These are recollections of one professional, rather than evidence that everyone entering a PC room wanted the same career. They connect several activities that a software description leaves apart: practising, learning from opponents, being watched and becoming recognisable to an audience gathered around the game and its players.

A contemporary Blizzard notice records another use of a PC bang nearly two decades later. For StarCraft: Remastered's 2017 Korean preview, the company invited adults to Gameinus's Sinnonhyeon location in Seoul. The planned evening combined a broadcast of the launch event with overnight play, individual and team tournaments, and invited broadcaster matches. This was a specifically organised gathering, not a description of every café's normal routine. Its programme placed watching and playing in the same venue, allowing one activity to lead into the next.

The announcement also specified its boundaries: registration, a limited attendance selected by lottery, identification checks and an event running beyond the hours when minors could enter. Free overnight access was part of that particular promotion. Those details show a room managed by rules and schedules as well as by networked computers. They cannot establish where PC bangs first appeared or explain their whole history. They do preserve an example of a shared gaming space being used to stage a collective occasion around a game.
